title: Create Your First Seaborn Heatmap
markdown:
### The Scenario
A retail team wants a compact view of weekly sales across stores.

### The Task
- Use `sns.heatmap()` to visualize `sales_data`.
- Use the colormap `Blues`.
- Give the chart the title: `Weekly Sales Heatmap`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

sales_data = pd.DataFrame(
    [[22, 18, 25, 20], [28, 24, 30, 27],[26, 21, 29, 23]],
    index=['Store A', 'Store B', 'Store C'],
    columns=['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu']
)

# Create your heatmap below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.collections) > 0, 'We could not find a heatmap. Did you use sns.heatmap()?'
assert ax.collections[0].cmap.name == 'Blues', 'Your heatmap should use the Blues colormap.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Weekly Sales Heatmap', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Weekly Sales Heatmap.'

title: Plot a Correlation Heatmap
markdown:
### The Scenario
A data analyst wants to inspect how several study-related variables relate to one another.

### The Task
- Compute the correlation matrix of `df`.
- Plot it with `sns.heatmap()`.
- Use `annot=True`.
- Use the colormap `coolwarm`.
- Set `center=0`.
- Give the chart the title: `Correlation Heatmap`.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'study_hours':[2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7],
    'sleep_hours':[8, 7, 7, 6, 6, 5],
    'practice_tests':[1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3],
    'exam_score':[60, 65, 72, 78, 85, 90]
})

# Create your correlation heatmap below

plt.show()
validation_code:

assert len(ax.texts) >= 16, 'We expected annotations on the correlation heatmap.'

title: Add Cell Borders to a Heatmap
markdown:
### The Scenario
An operations manager wants a clearer productivity heatmap with visible cell boundaries.

### The Task
- Use `sns.heatmap()` to visualize `productivity`.
- Use the colormap `rocket`.
- Set `linewidths=0.5`.
- Set `linecolor='white'`.
- Keep the color bar visible.
- Give the chart the title: `Team Productivity Heatmap`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

productivity = pd.DataFrame(
    [[72, 75, 78, 74],[68, 70, 73, 71], [80, 82, 85, 83],[76, 77, 79, 78]],
    index=['Team A', 'Team B', 'Team C', 'Team D'],
    columns=['Week 1', 'Week 2', 'Week 3', 'Week 4']
)

# Create your bordered heatmap below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.collections) > 0, 'We could not find a heatmap. Did you use sns.heatmap()?'
assert ax.collections[0].cmap.name == 'rocket', 'Your heatmap should use the rocket colormap.'
assert ax.collections[0].get_linewidths()[0] == 0.5, 'Your heatmap should use linewidths=0.5.'
assert len(fig.axes) == 2, 'We expected the heatmap and its color bar to be visible.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Team Productivity Heatmap', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Team Productivity Heatmap.'

title: Format Heatmap Annotations
markdown:
### The Scenario
A retailer wants a heatmap of store traffic with whole-number annotations only.

### The Task
- Use `sns.heatmap()` to visualize `traffic`.
- Turn on annotations with `annot=True`.
- Format the annotations as whole numbers with `fmt='.0f'`.
- Use the colormap `magma`.
- Give the chart the title: `Store Traffic Heatmap`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

traffic = pd.DataFrame(
    [[120, 135, 128], [142, 150, 147],[160, 158, 165]],
    index=['Store A', 'Store B', 'Store C'],
    columns=['Morning', 'Afternoon', 'Evening']
)

# Create your formatted heatmap below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.collections) > 0, 'We could not find a heatmap. Did you use sns.heatmap()?'
assert ax.collections[0].cmap.name == 'magma', 'Your heatmap should use the magma colormap.'
assert len(ax.texts) == 9, 'We expected annotations for all 9 cells.'
assert all('.' not in text.get_text() for text in ax.texts), 'Your annotations should be formatted as whole numbers.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Store Traffic Heatmap', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Store Traffic Heatmap.'

title: Create a Masked Correlation Heatmap
markdown:
### The Scenario
A data scientist wants to show only the lower triangle of a correlation matrix.

### The Task
- Compute the correlation matrix of `metrics`.
- Create an upper-triangle mask with `np.triu()`.
- Plot the heatmap with `sns.heatmap()` using that mask.
- Turn on annotations with `annot=True`.
- Use the colormap `viridis`.
- Set `square=True`.
- Turn the color bar off with `cbar=False`.
- Give the chart the title: `Masked Correlation Heatmap`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    'speed':[10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20],
    'accuracy':[70, 72, 75, 79, 82, 85],
    'stamina':[55, 58, 60, 64, 68, 70],
    'focus':[65, 67, 70, 73, 77, 80]
})

# Create your masked heatmap below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
fig = plt.gcf()
assert len(ax.collections) > 0, 'We could not find a heatmap. Did you use sns.heatmap()?'
assert ax.collections[0].cmap.name == 'viridis', 'Your heatmap should use the viridis colormap.'
assert len(fig.axes) == 1, 'The color bar should be turned off, so we expected only one axis.'
assert len(ax.texts) == 6, 'We expected annotations only on the visible lower-triangle cells.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Masked Correlation Heatmap', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Masked Correlation Heatmap.'
